title: Public Key Pinning Extension for HTTP
summary: This document defines a new HTTP header that lets web host operators tell browsers to remember (pin) the host's cryptographic identity for a period of time. During that time the browser requires the host to present a certificate matching the pins, which reduces the risk from mis-issued certificates.

plainLanguage.summary: A website tells your browser: remember my ID card details, and be suspicious if someone shows up with a different one later.

subtitle: How a website tells browsers which public keys to expect in its certificate chain on future visits.

tldr.problem: Any certification authority can vouch for any domain, so a compromised or mistaken authority can enable man-in-the-middle attacks on a site's users.
tldr.mechanism: The site sends a Public-Key-Pins header with SHA-256 fingerprints of public keys (pins) and a max-age. For that time the browser requires the site's certificate chain to contain a key matching one of the pins, and refuses the connection otherwise.
tldr.outcome: Host operators can limit which authorities can vouch for them, but pinning is trust-on-first-use and a wrong pin can lock users out, so the RFC demands a backup pin and care.

today: RFC 7469 is a Proposed Standard, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. The text itself calls for care because pinning is trust-on-first-use and a bad pin can make a site unreachable.

sections.title: The Idea of Key Pinning
sections.content:
This RFC defines an HTTP header that lets a user agent (UA, such as a browser) learn which Subject Public Key Info (SPKI) structures will appear in a web host's certificate chain in future TLS connections. A Pin is a relationship between a hostname and a cryptographic identity, here one or more public keys in a chain of X.509 certificates. Pin Validation is the check a UA performs to make sure the host really authenticates with its earlier Pin. The RFC says pinning is meant to be used with HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS), though keys can be pinned without HSTS.

Pinning is a trust-on-first-use mechanism. On the first connection the UA has nothing to validate against and can apply only its normal certificate validation. A man-in-the-middle (MITM) on that first connection cannot be detected, and could even inject its own pinning header. The RFC admits this is not a perfect defense, but says it still gives host operators a way to limit how many certification authorities can vouch for them, and lets UAs detect later in-process MITM attacks.

The RFC warns that deploying pinning safely needs operational and organizational maturity, because a host that pins to keys that become invalid can make itself unavailable.
sections.plainLanguage: The first time you meet someone, you have to take their word for who they are. After that you remember their face, and you can spot a fake who tries to pretend to be them.

sections.title: The Pinning Header Fields
sections.content:
There are two response headers: Public-Key-Pins (PKP) and Public-Key-Pins-Report-Only (PKP-RO). Both are lists of directives separated by semicolons. Directive names are case insensitive, order does not matter, and a directive MUST NOT appear twice (except pin directives). UAs MUST ignore headers that do not match the syntax and MUST ignore directives they do not recognize, and must not try to fix malformed headers.

The directives are:

  • pin-sha256="...": a base64-encoded SPKI fingerprint. SHA-256 is the only hash algorithm allowed at this time.
  • max-age: the number of seconds after receiving the header during which the UA SHOULD treat the host as a Known Pinned Host. It is REQUIRED in Public-Key-Pins and meaningless in the report-only header.
  • includeSubDomains: optional, valueless; extends the policy to the host's subdomains.
  • report-uri: optional; where the UA SHOULD POST Pin Validation failure reports.

When a connection passes Pin Validation using the Pins the UA has noted, the host becomes a Known Pinned Host.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is a note from the website with a list of key fingerprints, how long to remember them, and optionally where to send a complaint if something looks wrong.

sections.title: What a Pin Is
sections.content:
An SPKI Fingerprint is the output of a cryptographic hash whose input is the DER-encoded ASN.1 form of the Subject Public Key Info of an X.509 certificate. A Pin is the hash algorithm identifier plus that fingerprint, base64-encoded for use in a header. In this version only SHA-256 (sha256) is defined, and UAs MUST ignore Pins with algorithms they do not recognize while still processing the rest of the header.

Public keys are pinned instead of whole certificates, so operators can generate new certificates that contain old public keys. A key whose SPKI is incomplete in isolation, for example a DSA key without domain parameters, cannot be pinned.
sections.plainLanguage: A fingerprint is a short code made from a website's secret-matching public key. Two different keys give different codes, so the code works like a fingerprint for the key.

sections.title: How Browsers Note and Store Pins
sections.content:
A host sends the header over secure transport. Pinned Hosts SHOULD NOT send PKP over plain HTTP, and UAs MUST ignore a PKP header received over non-secure transport. UAs also MUST NOT heed http-equiv settings on meta elements.

The UA MUST note the Pins if and only if three conditions hold: the header arrived over an error-free TLS connection; that connection's certificate chain contains at least one SPKI matching a given fingerprint; and the pin set contains at least one Pin that does NOT refer to a key in the chain, which is the Backup Pin. A header meeting these conditions is a Valid Pinning Header, and the newest one replaces the stored Pins, expiration and report-uri.

The UA stores the domain name, the expiration (pin date plus max-age), whether includeSubDomains is set, and the report-uri. A max-age of 0 removes the stored policy. Hosts are identified by domain names only, never by IP addresses. UAs MAY cap max-age; the RFC's example is a 60 day cap of 5,184,000 seconds applied to a 90 day request.

The report-only header works differently: the UA MUST NOT cache information from it, and may evaluate it only to decide whether to send a report. A server may send both headers, and the PKP header is enforced.
sections.plainLanguage: The browser only writes down the pins if the visit looked safe and the site also lists a spare key. It then keeps the note until the time runs out.

sections.title: Pin Validation on Later Visits
sections.content:
When a UA connects to a Known Pinned Host over TLS and the connection has errors, it MUST terminate the connection without letting the user proceed anyway. If the connection is error-free, the UA SHOULD perform Pin Validation, and MUST do so before starting an HTTP conversation if it previously noted the host.

To validate, the UA computes the SPKI fingerprint of every certificate in the validated chain with each hash algorithm it supports, and checks that this set intersects the host's stored fingerprints. If it does, the connection continues. If not, the UA MUST treat the failure as a non-recoverable error. Local policy may disable validation, for example when the chain ends at a user-defined trust anchor, and in that case the UA SHOULD NOT send reports.
sections.plainLanguage: On each return visit the browser checks the site's key against its notes. If nothing matches, it slams the door and does not let you in.

sections.title: Failure Reports
sections.content:
If the host set report-uri, the UA SHOULD report Pin Validation failures by POSTing a JSON message to that URI. The report has the keys date-time, hostname, port, effective-expiration-date, include-subdomains, noted-hostname, served-certificate-chain, validated-certificate-chain and known-pins. Each key MUST appear once, and times use the RFC 3339 format. Certificates are given as PEM strings.

Reporting is best effort. If the report-uri host itself fails validation, the UA must cancel the connection, and if two pinned hosts name each other as report-uri, the UA SHOULD break the loop. UAs SHOULD limit how often they send reports.
sections.plainLanguage: If the browser catches a fake, it can mail a short note about it to an address the website gave, so the owner finds out something is wrong.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
There is a trade-off between pin specificity and resilience. If an operator pinned only the end-entity key and lost it, UAs would refuse the site for the whole max-age. Pinning keys of an intermediate issuer or trust anchor still narrows who can issue certificates for the host while leaving room to change keys.

The main safety net is the Backup Pin: a fingerprint for a not-yet-deployed key pair kept offline. UAs MUST require that hosts set one. The cost is that if an attacker gets that backup key, they can mount a MITM attack undetected.

On max-age, the RFC says there is probably no ideal limit, but about 60 days (5,184,000 seconds) may balance the concerns. Using includeSubDomains can break sibling subdomains with different pins, depending on which host the UA visits first. Hosts should also mark sensitive cookies secure and scope the domain attribute. Finally, an attacker with a validly issued certificate can attempt hostile pinning, which is limited by the maximum max-age and can be reduced by preloading pins in the UA.
sections.plainLanguage: If you lose your only key, you are locked out. So you hide a spare key somewhere safe. But a thief who finds the spare can also get in.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Hosts can use pinning, like HSTS, as a super-cookie to track browsers. In one scenario a site sets a made-up value as a "pin" and later reads it back through the failure report. In another, it serves pin headers from many subdomains to some browsers and not others, then sees which later connections fail. With N subdomains it can tell apart 2^N browsers.

Because UAs must store which domains set policies, the RFC advises that UAs let privacy-sensitive users clear and inspect pins, and notes that someone with physical access to a device may recover visited hosts. Failure reports can also reveal details of an organization's TLS interception tools. Section 7 adds that users who hit a pin failure experience denial of service, so UAs should explain why.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky website could hide a secret number in your browser's pin notes to recognize you later, even if you cleared your cookies.
